title: Commercial Lease Negotiation Checklist: 15 Points to Negotiate Before You Sign
description: A practical 15-point checklist covering every major negotiation lever in a commercial lease - from base rent and TI to CAM caps, renewal options, and exit rights.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What is the most important thing to negotiate in a commercial lease?
faq.answer: The single most important negotiation point depends on your situation, but for most tenants the CAM cap - a ceiling on annual operating expense increases - has the highest long-term dollar value. A 5-year lease without a CAM cap can expose you to unlimited operating expense growth; a 3% controllable expense cap on the same lease limits that growth to 34% over 10 years. For tenants with significant capital at risk (major buildouts, expensive equipment), a robust termination right or co-tenancy clause may be more important. For short-term financial flexibility, free rent and TI allowance have the most immediate impact.

faq.question: Can I negotiate a commercial lease without a broker?
faq.answer: You can, but you are at a significant information disadvantage. Tenant representative brokers have market data on comparable transactions, know the building's vacancy history, and have negotiated dozens of leases against many of the same landlords. More importantly, tenant rep services are typically paid by the landlord - the commission is built into the transaction economics regardless of whether you have representation. If you decline to use a tenant rep, the landlord keeps the full commission rather than paying half to your representative. You get no savings and no professional advocacy. For any lease with total value above $100,000, use a tenant rep.

faq.question: How long does commercial lease negotiation take?
faq.answer: A straightforward commercial lease negotiation for a small-to-mid-size tenant typically takes 4 to 12 weeks from initial proposal to signed lease. Complex negotiations for larger spaces, significant buildouts, or properties with unusual issues can take 3 to 6 months. The negotiation stages are: (1) landlord proposal or RFP response, 1-2 weeks; (2) letter of intent negotiation, 2-4 weeks; (3) lease document drafting and review, 3-6 weeks; (4) execution and delivery. The LOI stage is where the core business terms are agreed and is typically the highest-leverage phase of the negotiation.

title: Commercial Lease Renewal Negotiation: How to Get Better Terms the Second Time
description: Lease renewal is your best negotiating opportunity as a tenant. Learn when to start, what to ask for, and how to use market data to lower your rent and improve terms.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: When should I start negotiating my commercial lease renewal?
faq.answer: Start 12 to 18 months before your lease expiration date. This gives you enough time to genuinely evaluate alternatives - tour competing spaces, get competitive proposals, and use that market intelligence as leverage. Tenants who start 3 months before expiration negotiate from weakness: the landlord knows you cannot realistically move, so your threat to relocate is not credible. Starting 12–18 months out makes the threat credible and gives you time to actually exercise it if the landlord does not negotiate meaningfully.

faq.question: What will landlords typically negotiate on a lease renewal?
faq.answer: Landlords will generally negotiate on: free rent (1–3 months is common in soft markets), tenant improvement allowance to refresh the space, CAM cap resets or new caps if the original lease had none, renewal option language, and sometimes base rent reduction if the market has softened since the original lease. Landlords are least flexible on: lease term (they want longer terms), personal guarantee (they want to keep it), and structural lease provisions. The items landlords are most flexible on vary significantly by market conditions - a landlord with 15% vacancy negotiates very differently than one with 2% vacancy.

faq.question: How much does a tenant rep broker cost for lease renewal?
faq.answer: Tenant rep brokers for commercial lease renewals are typically paid by the landlord out of the transaction commission - there is no direct cost to the tenant in most cases. The broker's commission on a renewal is typically 2–4% of the total lease value (sometimes split with a landlord rep). For a 5-year renewal at $10,000/month, the total lease value is $600,000, and a tenant rep commission might be $12,000–$24,000, paid by the landlord. The tenant gets professional representation, market data, and negotiation expertise for free. Not using a tenant rep in a renewal negotiation is leaving professional leverage on the table.

title: How to Read a CAM Reconciliation Statement (and Spot Overcharges)
description: Your landlord's annual CAM reconciliation statement can include errors and inflated charges. Learn how to read every line item, what the gross-up provision means, and what to challenge.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: When does the landlord have to send the CAM reconciliation statement?
faq.answer: Most commercial leases require the landlord to deliver the annual CAM reconciliation statement within 90 to 120 days after the end of the calendar year - so by March 31 or April 30 for a December 31 fiscal year. Some leases specify 180 days. The deadline matters: if your lease contains a landlord default provision or a 'time is of the essence' clause tied to the reconciliation deadline, a late statement may limit the landlord's ability to collect additional amounts. Always note the deadline in your lease and flag any statements that arrive after it.

faq.question: How long do I have to dispute a CAM reconciliation statement?
faq.answer: Your lease's audit rights provision defines the dispute window - typically 12 to 18 months after receiving the reconciliation statement. Beyond this window, most leases deem the reconciliation final and binding. Do not let the audit window pass without at least reviewing the statement against your lease's expense definitions. If you identify potential overcharges, send a written notice of your intent to exercise audit rights before the window closes, even if the full audit is not complete.

faq.question: What is a gross-up provision in a CAM reconciliation statement?
faq.answer: A gross-up provision allows the landlord to calculate variable operating expenses as if the building were at a defined occupancy level - typically 90% to 95% - rather than actual occupancy. The rationale is that some operating expenses (property management, security, exterior lighting) are relatively fixed regardless of how many tenants are in the building. Without gross-up, tenants in a half-occupied building would bear an inflated share of fixed costs that will redistribute when the building fills. A proper gross-up applies only to variable expenses and only to the portion that genuinely varies with occupancy - not to every line item on the expense statement.

title: Types of Commercial Leases: NNN, Gross, Modified Gross, and Ground Leases Explained
description: The five main types of commercial leases - NNN, gross, modified gross, percentage, and ground - have very different cost structures and risk profiles. Here's how each works.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What is the most common type of commercial lease?
faq.answer: Triple net (NNN) leases are the most common structure for single-tenant retail, industrial, and net lease investment properties. Modified gross leases are the most common structure for multi-tenant office buildings, where the landlord covers structural expenses and the tenant pays for utilities and janitorial within their space. Pure gross leases are less common and typically found in smaller or older office buildings. Percentage leases are standard in enclosed shopping malls and food service retail. The 'most common' structure depends heavily on property type and market.

faq.question: Which type of commercial lease is best for a tenant?
faq.answer: A gross lease offers tenants the most cost predictability - one payment covers everything. But 'best' depends on your priorities. If you want to control your own maintenance and trade cost variability for a lower base rent, a NNN lease may result in lower total occupancy cost if the property is well-maintained and expenses are reasonable. The worst outcome for tenants is an uncapped NNN lease on a property with aging systems, where CAM charges escalate unpredictably. For most tenants without real estate expertise, a modified gross lease with clearly defined expense stops is the best balance of predictability and reasonable base rent.

faq.question: How can you tell what type of commercial lease you have from the lease document?
faq.answer: The lease type is usually identified in the recitals or in the base rent section. Look for language like 'triple net,' 'NNN,' 'gross lease,' or 'modified gross.' More reliably, look at the operating expense provisions: if the tenant is responsible for property taxes, insurance, and maintenance on top of base rent, it is NNN. If the tenant pays only base rent and the landlord covers operating expenses, it is gross. If there is an expense stop - 'Tenant pays operating expenses in excess of $X per square foot' - it is likely a modified gross or base year gross lease. If no clear language appears, read the expense allocation provisions carefully and classify based on who actually pays what.

title: What Is a Commercial Lease? Key Terms, Types, and What to Watch For
description: A commercial lease is a legally binding contract between a landlord and a business tenant. Learn the key terms, lease types, and critical clauses before you sign.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What makes a commercial lease different from a residential lease?
faq.answer: Commercial leases are largely unregulated compared to residential leases. There is no federal framework governing commercial lease terms - no implied warranty of habitability, no mandated notice periods, no automatic renewal protections. Everything is negotiated. A residential tenant has statutory protections even when they sign a terrible lease; a commercial tenant has only the rights they negotiate into the document itself. This makes reading and understanding the lease before signing critically important.

faq.question: How long is a typical commercial lease?
faq.answer: Commercial lease terms vary significantly by property type and tenant size. Retail leases commonly run 5 to 10 years with renewal options. Office leases in Class A buildings typically run 5 to 7 years for smaller tenants and 10 to 15 years for larger floor tenants. Industrial and warehouse leases often run 3 to 10 years. Ground leases run 30 to 99 years. Short-term (1–3 year) commercial leases exist primarily in flex space and coworking contexts, but standard market leases are 5-year minimum to justify landlord tenant improvement contributions.

faq.question: What happens if a landlord breaches a commercial lease?
faq.answer: Commercial lease remedies for landlord breach are governed by the lease itself and applicable state law. Common landlord breaches include failure to maintain the building, failure to deliver quiet enjoyment, violation of exclusive use provisions, and improper CAM charges. A tenant's remedies typically include: sending written notice of default and giving the landlord a cure period (usually 30 days), withholding rent only if the lease explicitly permits it and state law allows it, seeking specific performance in court, or terminating the lease if the breach is material. Never withhold rent without legal advice - in most states, rent withholding without proper procedure triggers a tenant default.

title: CAM Reconciliation: How the Annual Process Works
description: CAM reconciliation compares estimated vs. actual operating expenses in NNN leases. Learn the timeline, how to read a statement, common errors, and how to dispute overcharges.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What is CAM reconciliation?
faq.answer: CAM reconciliation is the annual process of comparing the estimated common area maintenance charges collected from tenants throughout the year against the landlord's actual operating expenses. If actual expenses exceeded estimates, tenants owe additional payment (true-up). If actual expenses were lower than estimates, tenants receive a credit or refund. Most NNN and modified gross leases require the landlord to complete reconciliation and deliver a statement within 90–120 days after the lease year ends.

faq.question: How does CAM reconciliation work?
faq.answer: CAM reconciliation works in four steps: (1) During the year, tenants pay monthly CAM estimates based on the landlord's projection. (2) After year-end, the landlord totals all actual operating expenses in the CAM pool. (3) The landlord calculates each tenant's pro-rata share of actual expenses and subtracts the estimates already paid. (4) Tenants with a positive balance (underpaid) receive a bill; tenants with a negative balance (overpaid) receive a credit or refund, depending on the lease terms.

faq.question: When is CAM reconciliation due?
faq.answer: Most commercial leases require CAM reconciliation statements to be delivered 90–120 days after the end of the lease year (which may be calendar year or lease anniversary year). A landlord who misses this deadline may forfeit the right to collect underpayments for that year - this provision is included in well-negotiated tenant-favorable leases. Tenants should track the reconciliation deadline and send a written notice if the statement is late.

faq.question: How do I read a CAM reconciliation statement?
faq.answer: A CAM reconciliation statement has four components: (1) Total operating expenses - the list of all costs incurred in the CAM pool during the year, with line items by category. (2) Gross-up calculation - if the lease allows expense gross-up, the adjustment to normalize expenses to a defined occupancy level. (3) Your pro-rata share - your rentable SF divided by total building rentable SF (or grossed-up area). (4) Reconciliation - your share of actual expenses minus your estimated payments, yielding the amount owed or the credit amount.

faq.question: What is a CAM reconciliation audit?
faq.answer: A CAM reconciliation audit is a formal examination of the landlord's expense records to verify that the amounts billed in the reconciliation statement match actual, lease-eligible expenses. Tenants have the right to audit under most NNN leases within 12 to 18 months of receiving the reconciliation statement. CAM audits can surface billing errors in the landlord-prepared reconciliation when charges do not match the lease. If the recovery exceeds the threshold specified in the lease, the landlord may be required to pay the tenant's audit costs.

faq.question: What is a commercial lease audit?
faq.answer: A commercial lease audit is a systematic review of a commercial lease and the landlord's associated charges to verify that billing, administration, and operating expense pass-throughs match what the lease contractually requires. It covers CAM reconciliation accuracy, rent escalation calculations, lease term compliance, and critical date tracking. Most lease audits are triggered by CAM reconciliation statements that show unexpected charges, but proactive audits at lease signing prevent overpayments from the start.

faq.question: How do you audit a commercial lease?
faq.answer: Auditing a commercial lease involves four steps: (1) Obtain a structured abstract of the lease identifying the exact contractual requirements for rent, CAM, escalation, and expense definitions. (2) Gather all landlord billing records - reconciliation statements, invoices, property tax bills, insurance certificates. (3) Compare actual charges against lease requirements line by line, identifying any expense that falls outside the permitted CAM definition, any calculation methodology inconsistency, or any fee above a capped rate. (4) Document findings in a written audit report and present to the landlord for credit or correction.

faq.question: What is a lease audit checklist?
faq.answer: A lease audit checklist covers: rent escalation calculations (verified against the lease schedule), CAM expense eligibility (each line item against the CAM definition), management fee vs. lease cap, pro-rata share denominator accuracy, gross-up calculation methodology, operating expense exclusions (capital expenditures, insurance-covered costs, other tenant costs), reconciliation statement delivery deadline, audit rights window status, and critical date compliance (renewal notice deadlines, TI draw deadlines, lease expiration).

faq.question: When should you audit a commercial lease?
faq.answer: The most productive times to audit a commercial lease: (1) At lease signing - use AI abstraction to extract all contractual terms and build a complete data baseline before any charges are incurred. (2) Annual CAM reconciliation - within the audit rights window (typically 12–18 months of receiving the statement). (3) Before lease renewal - audit the full lease term for accumulated overcharges, which strengthens renewal negotiating position. (4) Before lease assignment or sale - verify all landlord obligations have been met and no outstanding disputes exist.

title: Triple Net Lease (NNN): How It Works, What's Included & Calculator

faq.question: What is a triple net lease?
faq.answer: A triple net lease (NNN lease) is a commercial lease structure in which the tenant pays base rent plus three additional expense categories: property taxes, building insurance, and maintenance/repairs. In a true NNN lease, the tenant bears all operating costs of the property above the base rent, making the landlord's income nearly passive. Triple net leases are most common in single-tenant retail properties, net lease investment properties, and industrial facilities.

faq.question: How does a triple net lease work?
faq.answer: In a triple net lease, the landlord charges a lower base rent reflecting that the tenant covers operating expenses directly. The tenant pays monthly base rent plus estimated property tax and insurance amounts (often escrowed and reconciled annually) plus maintenance costs as incurred. At year end, the landlord reconciles actual expenses against estimates and the tenant pays any shortfall or receives a credit. The landlord's cash flow is predictable and close to passive; the tenant's total occupancy cost fluctuates with actual expenses.

faq.question: What is included in a triple net lease?
faq.answer: A triple net lease includes three expense categories beyond base rent: (1) property taxes - the tenant pays their proportional share of real estate taxes on the property; (2) building insurance - the tenant pays their share of the landlord's property, casualty, and liability insurance premiums; (3) maintenance and repairs - the tenant covers common area maintenance (CAM) including parking lots, landscaping, roofing, and building systems. In a true NNN lease, structural repairs and capital expenditures may also fall to the tenant.

faq.question: What is the difference between a triple net lease and a gross lease?
faq.answer: In a triple net lease, the tenant pays base rent plus property taxes, insurance, and maintenance expenses - total occupancy cost is higher than base rent and fluctuates with actual expenses. In a gross lease, the tenant pays a single all-inclusive rent and the landlord covers all operating expenses from that payment. NNN leases have lower base rents but variable total cost; gross leases have higher base rents but predictable total cost. For landlords, NNN leases provide more stable net income; for tenants, gross leases provide more predictable budgeting.

faq.question: What is a triple net lease calculator?
faq.answer: A triple net lease calculator estimates a tenant's total annual occupancy cost by adding base rent to estimated NNN expenses. Basic formula: Annual NNN cost = (Base rent per SF × RSF) + (Property tax per SF × RSF) + (Insurance per SF × RSF) + (CAM per SF × RSF). For a 5,000 SF tenant with $15/SF base rent, $3/SF taxes, $1.50/SF insurance, and $4/SF CAM, total annual cost = $28.50/SF × 5,000 = $142,500, or approximately $11,875/month.

faq.answer: Most leases require tenants to dispute a CAM statement within 90–180 days of receipt, and to request an audit within 12–24 months of receipt. faq.answer: Expenses that should be excluded from CAM in a well-negotiated lease include: capital expenditures and major repairs, landlord's depreciation, leasing commissions and tenant improvement allowances, income taxes, costs covered by insurance proceeds, and costs attributable to other tenants' negligence. faq.question: How do you calculate NNN rent?
faq.answer: Total NNN occupancy cost = Base Rent + CAM Charges + Real Estate Taxes + Insurance (all expressed per square foot per year, then multiplied by your leased square footage). For example: $18.00 base + $4.50 CAM + $3.25 taxes + $0.60 insurance = $26.35/SF/year total. Divide by 12 for the monthly payment.

faq.question: What does $18.00 NNN mean in commercial real estate?
faq.answer: $18.00 NNN means the base rent is $18.00 per square foot per year, and you pay property taxes, insurance, and CAM charges on top of that. On a 5,000 SF space, base rent is $65,000/year ($7,500/month), but total occupancy cost with NNN expenses typically runs $24–$28/SF - meaning the actual monthly payment would be $10,000–$11,667.

faq.question: How much are CAM charges on a NNN lease?
faq.answer: CAM charges on a NNN lease typically range from $3–$8 per square foot per year depending on property type and market. Retail centers tend to run $4–$8/SF, suburban office is $4–$6/SF, and industrial is $1–$3/SF. These are estimates - actual CAM is reconciled to real expenses each year, so budget 10–15% above the initial estimate for potential reconciliation payments.

faq.question: Is gross or NNN better for tenants?
faq.answer: A gross lease is generally more predictable for tenants because operating costs are bundled into base rent. A NNN lease exposes tenants to variable operating costs (CAM, taxes, insurance) that can increase significantly year over year. However, NNN base rents are typically lower than gross rents, and tenants who negotiate hard CAM caps and exclusions can limit their upside exposure. The better structure depends on the specific terms negotiated.

faq.question: What is a typical NNN lease expense load?
faq.answer: The NNN expense load (CAM + taxes + insurance) typically runs $6–$14 per square foot per year in most US markets. Retail shopping center tenants often see the highest loads ($8–$14/SF). Industrial tenants pay the least ($2–$5/SF). Office tenants typically fall in the $5–$9/SF range. These numbers have increased meaningfully since 2022 due to property tax reassessments and rising insurance premiums.

faq.question: How do you calculate rent escalation?
faq.answer: Rent escalation is calculated based on the escalation type in the lease. For fixed percentage escalation: New rent = Current rent × (1 + escalation rate). Example: $10,000/month × 1.03 = $10,300 for a 3% annual increase. For CPI escalation: New rent = Base rent × (Current CPI ÷ Base year CPI). For step rent: The new amount is stated explicitly in the lease schedule - just read the applicable year's amount. Always identify which type applies before calculating.

faq.question: What is a typical rent escalation rate?
faq.answer: The most common fixed annual rent escalation rate in commercial leases is 3% per year, though rates of 2–4% are standard depending on market conditions and negotiating positions. CPI-based escalation is common in long-term ground leases and some office leases - CPI has averaged 2–4% annually over the past decade but spiked above 8% in 2022. Percentage rent escalations in retail leases typically trigger when gross sales exceed a natural breakpoint calculated from base rent divided by the percentage rent rate.

faq.question: What is a rent escalation clause?
faq.answer: A rent escalation clause is a lease provision that specifies how and when base rent increases over the lease term. The three main types are: (1) fixed percentage increases (e.g., 3% annually), (2) CPI-indexed increases tied to the Consumer Price Index, and (3) step rent schedules with specific amounts for each year. Without an escalation clause, base rent stays flat for the entire lease term - which benefits the tenant but is uncommon in institutional lease deals.

title: CAM Charges Explained: What They Are, What's Included & How to Calculate
description: CAM charges are monthly operating expense pass-throughs in NNN leases. Learn what's included, how to calculate your share, and how to dispute overcharges.
author: Angel Campa, Founder

faq.question: What are CAM charges?
faq.answer: CAM charges (common area maintenance charges) are monthly fees tenants pay in NNN and modified gross leases to cover their proportional share of operating expenses for shared areas - parking lots, lobbies, landscaping, elevators, and building systems. A tenant occupying 5% of a building pays 5% of all CAM-eligible expenses.

faq.question: What is included in CAM charges?
faq.answer: CAM charges typically include landscaping, parking lot maintenance, exterior lighting, janitorial for common areas, elevator maintenance, HVAC for shared spaces, property management fees, and security. What is excluded depends on the lease - tenants can negotiate to exclude capital expenditures, above-market management fees, and costs related to other tenants' spaces.

faq.question: How do you calculate CAM charges?
faq.answer: CAM charges are calculated by multiplying the tenant's pro-rata share (tenant's rentable square footage ÷ total building rentable square footage) by the total annual CAM expenses. For example, a 5,000 SF tenant in a 100,000 SF building with $500,000 in annual CAM pays $25,000 per year ($500,000 × 5%), or approximately $2,083 per month.

faq.question: What are excessive CAM charges?
faq.answer: Excessive CAM charges are landlord billings that exceed what the lease allows - including capital expenditures passed as operating expenses, management fees above the lease cap, costs not covered by the CAM definition, and expenses that should be covered by insurance. CAM audits can surface these errors by comparing invoices, contracts, allocations, and charge categories against the lease.

faq.question: Can a tenant refuse to pay CAM charges?
faq.answer: A tenant cannot simply refuse to pay CAM charges if they are contractually required by the lease, as doing so constitutes a lease default. The correct approach is to pay under protest and simultaneously exercise audit rights, request supporting documentation, and dispute specific line items. If the landlord confirms an overcharge, most leases require a credit or refund within 30–60 days.

faq.question: What is an estoppel certificate?
faq.answer: An estoppel certificate is a legally binding document in which a tenant certifies the current status of their lease - confirming the lease commencement and expiration dates, current rent amount, security deposit held, whether the landlord is in default, and any outstanding landlord obligations. It is used by landlords in property sale and refinancing transactions to give buyers and lenders verified lease status.

faq.question: What is a certificate of estoppel?
faq.answer: A certificate of estoppel is the same document as an estoppel certificate - the terms are used interchangeably. It is a tenant's written certification of their lease status, signed under penalty of legal estoppel: the tenant cannot later assert facts that contradict what they certified, even if those facts are true. Lenders and buyers rely on estoppel certificates as authoritative representations of lease status.

faq.question: Who signs an estoppel certificate?
faq.answer: The tenant signs the estoppel certificate - typically an authorized officer or executive with signing authority under the lease. If the tenant is a partnership or LLC, the certificate must be signed by a partner or manager with authority to bind the entity. Some leases require both the tenant and any guarantors to sign. The landlord does not sign the estoppel certificate.

faq.question: How long do you have to return an estoppel certificate?
faq.answer: Most commercial leases give tenants 10 to 30 days to execute and return an estoppel certificate after the landlord's request. Failing to return the certificate within the required time is a lease default in most leases, and some leases include a 'deemed correct' provision - meaning the landlord's form is considered accurate if the tenant fails to respond within the deadline.

faq.question: What is the difference between an estoppel certificate and SNDA?
faq.answer: An estoppel certificate certifies the current status of a lease for a buyer or lender - a point-in-time representation. An SNDA (Subordination, Non-Disturbance, and Attornment Agreement) is a three-party contract between landlord, tenant, and lender that governs what happens to the lease if the lender forecloses. Both are commonly requested together in financing transactions, but they serve different purposes.

description: TI allowances average $30-$120/sq ft depending on market and lease term. Learn how to negotiate a higher TI, structure the payment, and track it under ASC 842. Real-world examples.

faq.question: What is a tenant improvement allowance?
faq.answer: A tenant improvement allowance (TI allowance) is a landlord-funded contribution toward the cost of improving a commercial space to suit the tenant's specific needs. It is expressed as a dollar amount per rentable square foot (e.g., $60/RSF) and applied toward construction, MEP systems, finishes, and architectural fees. TI is not a gift - it is an economic component of the lease transaction that is underwritten based on the lease term, tenant credit, and market conditions.

faq.question: What is a reasonable tenant improvement allowance?
faq.answer: A reasonable tenant improvement allowance depends on property type and market. For Class A office space in major gateway markets (New York, San Francisco, Chicago), $80-$150 per RSF is typical for new leases. Secondary markets run $40-$80 per RSF. Retail TI ranges from $10-$100 per RSF depending on tenant credit. Industrial TI is typically $10-$30 per RSF for office-finish areas. Medical and life sciences space can reach $150-$200 per RSF due to specialized infrastructure.

faq.question: Do you have to pay back a tenant improvement allowance?
faq.answer: Tenants do not directly pay back TI allowance - it is funded by the landlord. However, the landlord recovers the TI cost through the rent stream over the lease term. Economically, a lease with higher TI and higher base rent costs the same as one with lower TI and lower base rent over the full term. If a tenant terminates the lease early, many leases require the tenant to repay a prorated portion of the unamortized TI as part of the termination fee.

faq.question: How is tenant improvement allowance taxed?
faq.answer: Under current IRS rules, TI allowances received by tenants are generally excluded from taxable income when used for improvements to the leased property (IRC Section 109 / 1019). Under ASC 842, TI allowances received from the landlord reduce the tenant's initial right-of-use (ROU) asset - they are treated as lease incentives that offset the initial measurement. Consult a tax advisor for your specific situation.

faq.question: What happens to unused tenant improvement allowance?
faq.answer: Unused TI allowance is typically forfeited at the draw deadline (usually 12-18 months after lease commencement) unless the lease specifically allows the tenant to apply unused funds to rent credits, FF&E, or other costs. Negotiate the use of unused TI allowance upfront - landlords have no incentive to agree to repurpose unused funds after the lease is signed.
